subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 5. In this unit you will explore one of the most exciting and fast-changing parts of computing today: artificial intelligence (AI) and the way digital devices store and use data. Every day you touch technology that seems almost clever. When a phone unlocks by looking at a face, when a search engine finishes your sentence, when a weather app warns a farmer near Baidoa that rain is coming, or when a message app suggests the next word in Somali or English, you are living with AI.

You will start by learning the difference between the two big families of software: systems software and application software. Then you will revisit what AI really means, discover how it is used across many industries, examine how digital data is stored as bits and bytes, and look closely at how image recognition lets a computer recognise objects in a picture. Along the way you will also meet logic gates, the tiny decision-makers hidden inside every digital device.

This is a self-paced unit. That means you move at your own speed. Everything in this unit can be explored with free, open-source software and the device you already own. You do not need to buy anything.

concepts.title: Systems Software and Application Software
concepts.explanation:
Every digital device needs software. Software is the word for the programs and instructions that tell a device how to complete a task. You cannot touch software; it is different from hardware, which is the physical part you can hold, such as the screen or the battery. All software falls into two main groups.

Systems software is the software that runs and manages the device itself. The most important piece of systems software is the operating system (OS). The operating system manages all the hardware, keeps programs running smoothly, and provides a user interface so you can interact with the machine. Without an operating system, the hardware would just be useless metal and glass. Examples of operating systems include Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS. On your own device, the OS is what you see the moment you switch it on, before you open anything.

Systems software also includes utility programs. These are small helper tools that keep the device healthy and safe, such as antivirus software, a file manager, a backup tool, or a program that cleans up unwanted files to free space. You rarely think about utilities, but they work quietly in the background.

Application software (often just called 'apps') is software that helps *you*, the user, carry out a task you actually want to do. Examples include a web browser, a word processor, a spreadsheet, an image editor, a calculator, a messaging app, a game, a maps app, or a camera app. Application software serves the user; systems software serves the machine. Both are needed. The OS is like the manager of a shop who keeps the lights on and the doors open; the applications are like the workers who serve each customer's particular request.

Here is a clear comparison you should learn well, because it is one of the main objectives of this unit.

Application packages such as the Google App Suite or Microsoft Office are called integrated applications. The programs inside them (documents, spreadsheets, slides) share a similar look and can pass data between each other, so once you learn one, the others feel familiar.

Feature — Systems software · Application software

Main job — Runs and manages the device and its hardware · Helps you do a specific task you want to do

Who it serves — Serves the computer and the other software · Serves you, the user

Examples — Operating systems (Windows, Android, Linux, iOS, macOS); utilities (antivirus, file manager, backup, disk cleanup) · Browser, word processor, spreadsheet, image editor, games, messaging apps, camera app

Needed to use the device? — Yes. Without the operating system the hardware is useless · No. The device still runs; you just cannot do that one task

concepts.title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
concepts.explanation:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is technology that lets a digital device act or think in a way that is similar to a human. AI can do tasks that we usually think need human intelligence, such as understanding speech, recognising images, driving a vehicle, translating languages, or answering questions in a conversation.

The key feature of modern AI is that it can learn from experience. This is called machine learning. Instead of a programmer writing a rule for every single situation, the AI is shown huge amounts of example data and finds the patterns by itself. A special type of machine learning called a neural network is loosely inspired by the way the human brain uses connected cells. Because it learns, an AI system can *improve over time*. A digital assistant recognises your voice more clearly the more you use it; a music app recommends songs closer to your taste; a keyboard predicts your next word more accurately.

It is important to be honest about what this 'intelligence' really is. An AI does not understand the world the way you do, and it does not have feelings, beliefs or a conscience. It is a very powerful pattern-finder built by people. Remembering this will help you judge when to trust it and when to think for yourself.

How an AI system works: input, process, output

Every AI system, no matter how clever, follows the same three-step model that all computers follow.

Input — the system collects data from its surroundings, for example a voice command through a microphone, a picture through a camera, or a reading from a sensor.

Process — the system analyses that data. For example, it analyses the voice pattern to work out the words, then follows its program to decide what to do.

Output — the system produces a result, such as switching a light on, reading out the weather, unlocking a phone, or displaying an answer on screen.

For example, when someone asks a digital assistant, 'What will the weather be like today?', the microphone captures the voice (input), a service analyses the sound and picks out the key words and looks up the forecast (process), and a spoken answer plays through the speaker (output). Keep this input-process-output pattern in your mind. You will use it to describe every AI system in this unit, including your Final Project.
concepts.example: Many people picture AI as walking, talking robots. In truth, most AI is invisible. It lives inside apps, smart heating systems, spam filters and cameras. A smart fridge, a bank's fraud checker and a phone's face unlock all use AI, and none of them looks like a robot.

concepts.title: AI Across Industries
concepts.explanation:
AI already affects how people live, work, shop and spend their free time. Companies and organisations collect large amounts of data and use AI to analyse it at high speed and make decisions automatically, without a human giving each instruction. Let us look at how AI helps in several industries, with examples close to home in East Africa.

Notice the common thread: an AI system takes in data, finds patterns, and makes or suggests a decision faster than a human could. This is why AI is so useful in industries that handle huge amounts of information.

A word that comes up again and again with AI is automate. To automate a task means to let a device complete it on its own, with little or no human help, by using sensors and program instructions. Automation is why AI is so valuable in industry: a system can watch, decide and act day and night without tiring. A device that uses sensors and connects to other devices is called a smart device, and the technology behind it is called smart technology (SMART stands for Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology).

When several smart devices in one house are connected together, often through a digital assistant and the internet, we call it a smart home. In a smart home a family might switch lights on and off, adjust the heating or cooling, or check a security camera, all from a single phone. Each of these actions still follows input, process, output. Think about how this could serve a household responsibly: a smart light that switches off automatically when a room is empty saves electricity and money, which is a responsible use of energy and resources. As you design your own AI system later in this unit, you will decide which sensors and outputs your smart device needs.

Industry — How AI is used · Example close to home

Agriculture and livestock — AI studies photos of leaves to spot crop disease early, predicts rainfall, and checks the health of animals. · An app that lets Sami photograph a sorghum leaf and warns him if it shows signs of disease before it spreads to the whole field.

Healthcare — AI helps doctors diagnose illness, plan treatment, and monitor patients using devices such as smart watches. · A rural clinic uses AI to read an X-ray and flag possible pneumonia, so a nurse knows which patients need a doctor first.

Transport — Driverless features and cameras use image recognition to read road signs, spot obstacles and react quickly. · AI traffic cameras in a growing city adjust the traffic lights when they detect a build-up of cars, easing the jam.

Business and finance — AI predicts future sales from past data, and spots unusual card activity to detect fraud. · A bank's AI notices a card being used in two distant places within minutes and sends the owner a warning text.

Retail and advertising — AI studies what people search for and buy, then targets adverts and suggestions at each person. · After Nadia searches online for a phone case, she suddenly sees adverts for phone cases in her apps.

Manufacturing — AI controls machines that build and package products with little human help. · A factory line fills and seals cans of food, or assembles parts, guided by an automated AI system.

Customer service — Chatbots answer common questions in a conversation, and pass harder ones to a human. · A travel website's chatbot answers Maya's question about a booking instantly, at any hour of the day.
concepts.example: Gaming — AI controls non-player characters (NPCs) and makes a game harder as the player improves. · A game gets tougher for Leo the more he plays, keeping it challenging and fun.

concepts.title: How AI Collects Data - Sensors
concepts.explanation:
AI systems need data before they can decide anything. Some data comes from a keyboard, a touchscreen or a microphone. A great deal of it, though, comes from sensors. A sensor is a device that gathers information from its surroundings and turns it into data the computer can process. Sensors are the 'senses' of a smart device.

Point a TV remote at your phone's camera and press a button. On the screen you may see a small purple or red flash. That is infrared light, invisible to your eyes but visible to the camera. Security systems use infrared sensors to detect people in the dark.

Sensor — Data it collects · Example use in an AI system

Temperature — Change in heat in the environment · Body-temperature scanners at an airport spot a possibly ill traveller and, combined with facial recognition, help prevent illness spreading.

Proximity — How close a nearby object is · A driverless car detects an obstacle in the road; a forklift warns a worker who is standing too close.

Infrared — Heat given off by an object, and invisible light · Drones with infrared cameras count endangered animals over remote land; security systems detect an intruder in the dark.

Humidity — Amount of water in the air · A smart cooling system keeps a building or a store of grain at a comfortable, safe moisture level.
concepts.example: Touch/pressure — How much force is applied to a surface · A robotic hand senses how hard it is gripping so it can pick up a date or an egg without crushing it.

concepts.title: How Image Recognition Works, Step by Step
concepts.explanation:
Image recognition is one of the most powerful uses of AI. It means a computer looking at a picture and identifying what is in it by studying the lines, colours, textures and shapes. Face unlock, driverless cars reading signs, and an app that spots crop disease all use image recognition. Here is how it works, step by step.

Capture the image. A camera or sensor takes a picture. As you will learn in Concept 6, the picture is stored as a grid of pixels, and each pixel's colour is written as a binary number.

Prepare the image. The system may resize the picture, adjust the brightness, or turn it into a standard format so that different images can be compared fairly.

Find the features. The AI scans the image for patterns: edges, corners, curves, colours and textures. It breaks a complex picture down into simple features. This is the computational-thinking skill of decomposition.

Compare with what it has learned. During its training the AI was shown thousands of labelled example pictures, for example many photos of ripe dates and unripe dates. It compares the features it found with the patterns it learned. This training is machine learning, often using a neural network.

Make a prediction. The system works out how confident it is for each possible answer and chooses the most likely one, for example 'this is a ripe date, 92 percent confident'.

Act on the result (output). The prediction is used to do something useful: unlock the phone, sort the dates into baskets, flag a diseased leaf, or read a car's number plate.

Learn and improve. When people confirm whether the answer was right or wrong, that feedback helps the model do better next time.

Think about Nadia sorting dates at the market. An image-recognition app could look at each date and sort it into 'ripe', 'unripe' or 'damaged' far faster than by hand. Or think about Sami: he photographs a leaf, and the app compares it with thousands of leaf images to warn him that a disease may be starting. Image recognition also keeps devices secure: face unlock still recognises you when you change your hair, wear glasses, or stand in poor light, because it learned the stable features of your face rather than one exact picture.

Image recognition is powerful, but it is not perfect, and a good computer scientist is honest about its limits. A model can only recognise things similar to the examples it was trained on. If it never saw a certain type of date, an unusual leaf disease, or a face in very dim light, it may guess wrongly, yet still report a high confidence. If the training pictures were unfair or incomplete, the system can be biased and treat some people or things unfairly. This is why serious uses, such as in a clinic or for security, keep a human in charge to check important decisions. The lesson is simple: let image recognition help you, but do not switch off your own judgement.

concepts.title: Representing and Storing Digital Data
concepts.explanation:
AI systems process images, sound, text and numbers. But a computer cannot store any of these the way you see them. Deep inside, a computer only understands binary: patterns of 1s and 0s. A single binary digit (a 1 or a 0) is called a bit. Everything — every photo, every song, every word — is turned into bits before a device can store or process it. When AI collects data from the world, that data is often analogue and must be converted into binary first.

Representing images: bitmap graphics

One way to store a picture is as a bitmap graphic (also called a raster image). A bitmap is made of tiny dots called pixels (short for 'picture element'), arranged on a grid. Each pixel is given a group of binary digits that describes its colour. In a picture using only black and white, each pixel needs just 1 bit: for example 1 for black and 0 for white.

The number of bits used per pixel is called the colour depth. More bits mean more possible colours. With a colour depth of 1 you get 2 colours. With a colour depth of 2 you get 4 colours (00, 01, 10, 11). With a colour depth of 8 you get 256 colours, and with 24 bits you get over 16 million colours — enough for a lifelike photograph. The number of pixels in the image is its resolution, measured in pixels per inch (ppi). Higher resolution means a sharper picture, but also more pixels, more bits and therefore a bigger file size.

To work out the storage for a bitmap, multiply the number of pixels by the colour depth. For a small picture that is 10 pixels wide and 10 pixels high with a colour depth of 1: (10 x 10) x 1 = 100 bits. If the same grid uses a colour depth of 2: (10 x 10) x 2 = 200 bits. If you zoom right into a bitmap on screen you can see the individual pixel squares, and each one can be edited or deleted.

Representing images: vector graphics

A second way to store an image is as a vector graphic. Instead of recording every pixel, a vector image stores a set of instructions describing shapes: draw a line of this length, place a circle here, fill this petal with this colour. Because it stores instructions rather than every dot, a vector image usually takes up less memory and can be resized without becoming blurry. Logos and simple diagrams are often vectors; detailed photographs are usually bitmaps.

Sound enters a computer as an analogue signal through a microphone. Because a computer cannot store analogue data, the sound wave is turned into binary by an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). Text is stored using a code that gives every character its own binary pattern. A common code is ASCII, where each character is stored in one byte (8 bits). For example, in ASCII the capital letter H is 01001000 and the capital letter O is 01001111. Each key you press sends its unique binary pattern to the processor, the part of the computer that carries out instructions.

Measuring data storage: from bits to terabytes

Because single bits are tiny, we group and scale them up. 8 bits make 1 byte, and one byte is roughly enough to store one character. The units then climb in big steps. Traditionally in computing each step is 1024 (which is 2 to the power of 10, because computers work in powers of two), although people often round this to about 1000 to keep the mental maths simple.

Strictly speaking, engineers now call 1000-byte units kilobytes (kB) and 1024-byte units kibibytes (KiB), to avoid confusion. At your level it is fine to learn that a byte is 8 bits and the units go up in steps of about a thousand. The important idea is that bigger files need more storage.

Storing a photo as millions of pixels, or as a set of shape instructions, are two different abstractions of the same picture. Choosing the right way to represent data for the job at hand is a key computing skill.

Unit — Size · Roughly enough for

Bit — 1 binary digit (0 or 1) · The answer to a single yes/no question

Byte — 8 bits · One character, such as the letter A

Kilobyte (KB) — 1024 bytes · A short paragraph of plain text

Megabyte (MB) — 1024 KB · A photo or about a minute of music

Gigabyte (GB) — 1024 MB · A long film in fairly good quality
concepts.example: Terabyte (TB) — 1024 GB · Thousands of films, or a huge photo library

concepts.title: Logic Gates and Boolean Logic
concepts.explanation:
How does a device actually 'decide' anything using only 1s and 0s? The answer is logic gates. A logic gate is a tiny circuit that takes one or two inputs and produces a single output. Inputs and outputs are electrical signals that are either ON or OFF, which is perfect for representing 1 or 0. Logic gates are the building blocks of every digital circuit, found in door bells, burglar alarms, street lights and the processor of your phone.

Logic gates work using Boolean logic, a kind of maths where every value is either true or false (1 or 0). A condition is a statement that is checked to see whether it is true or false. The three most common gates are AND, OR and NOT.

An AND gate has two inputs and outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1. Think of deciding whether you can make a cheese sandwich: you need bread AND cheese. Only when you have both can you make the sandwich.

An OR gate has two inputs and outputs 1 when either input is 1 (or both). Think of deciding whether to play a game online: you will play if friend A is online OR friend B is online. You are happy if either one, or both, are there.

A NOT gate is the simplest gate. It has only one input, and its output is always the opposite of the input. It is also called an inverter. Think of a home alarm: if you ARE in the house (1) the alarm is OFF (0); if you are NOT in the house (0) the alarm is ON (1).
concepts.example: For complex decisions, the output of one gate can become the input of another, forming a logic circuit. Every task your processor performs is built from millions of these tiny true/false operations happening incredibly fast.

concepts.title: A Balanced Look at Living with AI
concepts.explanation:
AI is powerful, and power always brings responsibility. A thoughtful person weighs the benefits against the risks rather than simply cheering or fearing. Here is a fair look at both sides.

Fewer errors and more accuracy — for example, AI has made weather forecasting more reliable, which helps farmers and fishers plan.

Always available — an AI can monitor a factory or answer a question at any hour, without tiring.

Faster decisions — a self-driving system can react to danger more quickly than a human in some situations.

Progress in research — AI helps discover medicines, plan where to build clinics, and study the environment.

Help for people who are excluded — AI can translate languages, read text aloud for people who cannot see well, and bring learning to remote places.

Cost — AI systems and the devices around them are expensive to build and maintain.

Jobs — because AI can work quickly and without breaks, some people worry it will replace human workers.

No feelings or wisdom — an AI decides using data and patterns only. It cannot truly understand a person's circumstances, mercy, or dignity.

Privacy — to work well, AI often collects a lot of personal data, sometimes through text files called cookies, without people fully realising.

Bias and mistakes — if an AI learns from unfair or incomplete data, it can make unfair or wrong decisions and still sound confident.

Over-reliance — if we trust AI blindly, we may stop thinking, checking and learning for ourselves.

You carry a helpful compass here: the shared values of honesty, fairness, responsibility and respect for others. Ask of any AI tool: Is it honest? Is it fair to everyone? Does it protect people's privacy and dignity? Does it help my community without causing harm? Technology is a tool; the responsibility for using it well belongs to the human being, not the machine. A good rule is to let AI *assist* your thinking, never *replace* it.

Researchers are trying to build AI that can respond to human emotions, sometimes called artificial empathy. Even so, a machine copying the signs of care is not the same as a human who truly cares. Real compassion still comes from people.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 2: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
workedExamples.prompt: Application software is best described as software that: (a) manages the hardware (b) starts automatically when you switch on (c) helps the user do a specific task (d) is impossible to remove
workedExamples.solution:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is technology that lets a digital device act or think in a way that is similar to a human. AI can do tasks that we usually think need human intelligence, such as understanding speech, recognising images, driving a vehicle, translating languages, or answering questions in a conversation.

The key feature of modern AI is that it can learn from experience. This is called machine learning. Instead of a programmer writing a rule for every single situation, the AI is shown huge amounts of example data and finds the patterns by itself. A special type of machine learning called a neural network is loosely inspired by the way the human brain uses connected cells. Because it learns, an AI system can *improve over time*. A digital assistant recognises your voice more clearly the more you use it; a music app recommends songs closer to your taste; a keyboard predicts your next word more accurately.

It is important to be honest about what this 'intelligence' really is. An AI does not understand the world the way you do, and it does not have feelings, beliefs or a conscience. It is a very powerful pattern-finder built by people. Remembering this will help you judge when to trust it and when to think for yourself.

How an AI system works: input, process, output

Every AI system, no matter how clever, follows the same three-step model that all computers follow.

Input — the system collects data from its surroundings, for example a voice command through a microphone, a picture through a camera, or a reading from a sensor.

Process — the system analyses that data. For example, it analyses the voice pattern to work out the words, then follows its program to decide what to do.

Output — the system produces a result, such as switching a light on, reading out the weather, unlocking a phone, or displaying an answer on screen.

For example, when someone asks a digital assistant, 'What will the weather be like today?', the microphone captures the voice (input), a service analyses the sound and picks out the key words and looks up the forecast (process), and a spoken answer plays through the speaker (output). Keep this input-process-output pattern in your mind. You will use it to describe every AI system in this unit, including your Final Project.

For example: Many people picture AI as walking, talking robots. In truth, most AI is invisible. It lives inside apps, smart heating systems, spam filters and cameras. A smart fridge, a bank's fraud checker and a phone's face unlock all use AI, and none of them looks like a robot.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 6: Representing and Storing Digital Data
workedExamples.prompt: How many bits are in one byte? (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 8 (d) 16
workedExamples.solution:
AI systems process images, sound, text and numbers. But a computer cannot store any of these the way you see them. Deep inside, a computer only understands binary: patterns of 1s and 0s. A single binary digit (a 1 or a 0) is called a bit. Everything — every photo, every song, every word — is turned into bits before a device can store or process it. When AI collects data from the world, that data is often analogue and must be converted into binary first.

Representing images: bitmap graphics

One way to store a picture is as a bitmap graphic (also called a raster image). A bitmap is made of tiny dots called pixels (short for 'picture element'), arranged on a grid. Each pixel is given a group of binary digits that describes its colour. In a picture using only black and white, each pixel needs just 1 bit: for example 1 for black and 0 for white.

The number of bits used per pixel is called the colour depth. More bits mean more possible colours. With a colour depth of 1 you get 2 colours. With a colour depth of 2 you get 4 colours (00, 01, 10, 11). With a colour depth of 8 you get 256 colours, and with 24 bits you get over 16 million colours — enough for a lifelike photograph. The number of pixels in the image is its resolution, measured in pixels per inch (ppi). Higher resolution means a sharper picture, but also more pixels, more bits and therefore a bigger file size.

To work out the storage for a bitmap, multiply the number of pixels by the colour depth. For a small picture that is 10 pixels wide and 10 pixels high with a colour depth of 1: (10 x 10) x 1 = 100 bits. If the same grid uses a colour depth of 2: (10 x 10) x 2 = 200 bits. If you zoom right into a bitmap on screen you can see the individual pixel squares, and each one can be edited or deleted.

Representing images: vector graphics

A second way to store an image is as a vector graphic. Instead of recording every pixel, a vector image stores a set of instructions describing shapes: draw a line of this length, place a circle here, fill this petal with this colour. Because it stores instructions rather than every dot, a vector image usually takes up less memory and can be resized without becoming blurry. Logos and simple diagrams are often vectors; detailed photographs are usually bitmaps.

Sound enters a computer as an analogue signal through a microphone. Because a computer cannot store analogue data, the sound wave is turned into binary by an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). Text is stored using a code that gives every character its own binary pattern. A common code is ASCII, where each character is stored in one byte (8 bits). For example, in ASCII the capital letter H is 01001000 and the capital letter O is 01001111. Each key you press sends its unique binary pattern to the processor, the part of the computer that carries out instructions.

Measuring data storage: from bits to terabytes

Because single bits are tiny, we group and scale them up. 8 bits make 1 byte, and one byte is roughly enough to store one character. The units then climb in big steps. Traditionally in computing each step is 1024 (which is 2 to the power of 10, because computers work in powers of two), although people often round this to about 1000 to keep the mental maths simple.

Strictly speaking, engineers now call 1000-byte units kilobytes (kB) and 1024-byte units kibibytes (KiB), to avoid confusion. At your level it is fine to learn that a byte is 8 bits and the units go up in steps of about a thousand. The important idea is that bigger files need more storage.

Storing a photo as millions of pixels, or as a set of shape instructions, are two different abstractions of the same picture. Choosing the right way to represent data for the job at hand is a key computing skill.

Unit — Size · Roughly enough for

Bit — 1 binary digit (0 or 1) · The answer to a single yes/no question

Byte — 8 bits · One character, such as the letter A

Kilobyte (KB) — 1024 bytes · A short paragraph of plain text

Megabyte (MB) — 1024 KB · A photo or about a minute of music

Gigabyte (GB) — 1024 MB · A long film in fairly good quality

For example: Terabyte (TB) — 1024 GB · Thousands of films, or a huge photo library

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

rules.title: ! AI
rules.text: AI follows input, process, output. It learns from data (machine learning), improves over time, but has no true feelings or understanding.

terms: Software
The programs and instructions that tell a device what to do. You cannot touch software.
Hardware
The physical parts of a device that you can touch, such as the screen, keyboard and battery.
Systems software
Software that runs and manages the device itself, for example the operating system.
Operating system
The most important systems software; it manages the hardware and lets you use other programs.
Application software
Software that helps you do a task you want to do, such as a browser or a camera app.
Artificial intelligence (AI)
Technology that lets a computer act or think in a way similar to a human.
Machine learning
A type of AI that learns and improves by finding patterns in large amounts of data.
Automate
To let a device complete a task on its own, with little or no human help.
Image recognition
A computer identifying objects by studying the lines, colours, textures and shapes in a picture.
Sensor
A device that gathers data from its surroundings, such as temperature, light or distance.
Binary
A number system using only 0 and 1; the only language a computer truly understands.
Bit
A single binary digit, either 0 or 1. The smallest piece of data.
Byte
A group of 8 bits. Enough to store one character, such as the letter A.
Pixel
Short for 'picture element'; one tiny dot in a bitmap image.
Logic gate
A tiny circuit that takes one or two inputs and produces a single output, using Boolean logic.
